stories.title: Walmart Building Supercenter in SE Tucson
stories.excerpt: Walmart Inc. plans to build a new Supercenter of more than 170,000 square feet at Houghton Town Center in southeast Tucson, following its $6.99 million acquisition of approximately 33.23 acres of commercial land. Diamond Ventures sold the property to Walmart Inc. Construction is expected to begin during the first quarter of 2027. The property is located at 10052 E. Old Vail Road near Walmart’s existing store at Houghton and Old Vail roads,. The existing Walmart store, which is owned by the retailer, will remain open until the new Supercenter launches. After Walmart vacates the current building, the space is expected to be repositioned and leased to two or three retailers. Shannon Murphy with CBRE represented the seller in the transaction. Besides the new Walmart, Houghton Town Center has The Home Depot, T.J. Maxx, Ross and Petco as tenants The post Walmart Building Supercenter in SE Tucson appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Walmart acquiring 33.23 acres, building 170K SF supercenter in SE Tucson Q1 2027
Existing Walmart vacates; current building to be repositioned to 2-3 new retailers
Houghton Town Center anchored by Home Depot, TJ Maxx, Ross, Petco
stories.summary: Walmart is building a new 170,000-square-foot supercenter at Houghton Town Center in southeast Tucson after paying $6.99 million for 33.23 acres. Construction begins Q1 2027. The existing store will close once the new location opens, and the vacated building will be repositioned for 2–3 new retail tenants. The submarket is already anchored by Home Depot, TJ Maxx, Ross, and Petco.
stories.impact: Retail-focused development signals continued retail investment in SE Tucson's Houghton corridor, but minimal direct demand driver for multifamily. However, the 2-3 new retailers moving into the existing space may generate secondary job/service worker demand; monitor whether Tucson's population growth (modest but steady) creates pent-up rental demand as retail footprint expands.

stories.title: Fashion House Veronica Beard Expands HQ to 60K SF at 26 West 17th Street
stories.excerpt: Apparel retail brand Veronica Beard has expanded its office headquarters to approximately 60,000 square feet at the Winter Organization’s 26 West 17th Street in Midtown South, according to landlord broker CBRE. The company, which has been in the building since about 2013, signed the new deal to renew its existing space at the building and also grow by 15,000 square feet. It will now occupy space on the second and third floors, as well as on the fifth through eighth floors of the office building two blocks west of Union Square. The asking rent and the length of the lease expansion were not disclosed. The average asking rent for office space in Midtown South was $79.41 per square foot during the second quarter of 2026, according to data from Colliers. David Stockel and Taylor Walker from CBRE represented ownership in the deal. “Veronica Beard’s decision to renew and expand its footprint at 26 West 17th Street demonstrates confidence in both the location and its future growth trajectory,” Stockel said in a statement. “The transaction highlights continued demand from established tenants for high-quality office environments that support collaboration, culture and business expansion.” JLL’s TJ Hochanadel and Robert Martin handled things on behalf of Veronica Beard. “Veronica Beard has grown its business at 26 West 17th Street since establishing its first office there,” Martin told Commercial Observer. “We aligned their real estate strategy with their business trajectory, and as they continued scaling, a more sustainable long-term solution became necessary.” Veronica Beard is led by sisters-in-law Veronica Miele Beard and Veronica Swanson Beard. The brand has retail stores in New York at 41 Grand Street in SoHo and 988 Madison Avenue on the Upper East Side. Built in 1907, 26 West 17th Street is a 12-story office building with tenants including wholesale marketplace Faire and energy equipment and solutions provider Scale Microgrids.
bullets: Veronica Beard renews and expands HQ to 60K SF at 26 West 17th, Midtown South Manhattan
Company adds 15K SF, occupying floors 2-3 and 5-8 since 2013; Midtown South asking rent $79.41/SF Q2 2026
Apparel brand expansion signals tenant confidence in postwar office location west of Union Square
stories.summary: Fashion brand Veronica Beard has renewed and expanded its Manhattan headquarters to 60,000 square feet at 26 West 17th Street in Midtown South, adding 15,000 square feet to its existing footprint. The company now occupies floors 2–3 and 5–8 of the Winter Organization building, which it has occupied since 2013. Midtown South average office rents are $79.41 per square foot as of Q2 2026.
stories.impact: Minimal impact on multifamily development. Office tenant expansion in Midtown South reflects some stabilization in Manhattan office markets, but conversion-to-residential pipelines (see Article 10) are more relevant to multifamily supply. Apparel/retail HQ expansion does not directly signal apartment demand in the submarket.

stories.title: Morgan Stanley Affiliate Pays $59M for Chandler Honeywell Aerospace Plant
stories.excerpt: A Morgan Stanley affiliate paid $59 million for a nearly 200,000-square-foot building in Chandler where Honeywell Aerospace has been a tenant since 2020. The industrial park, Amplify Chandler, was sold by Phoenix Rising Investments. JLL brokers Ben Geelan and Greer Oliver represented the seller. The Phoenix Business Journal reports Morgan Stanley Real Estate Investing was interested in the site because of its infill location, proximity to a strong manufacturing base, power infrastructure and credit tenants. Phoenix Rising Investments acquired the building in 2019. Honeywell moved in the following year, in April 2020. Since acquiring the site, Honeywell have invested roughly $150 million in renovations and expansions over the years, turning a former empty back-office building into a site for advanced manufacturing. A 40,000-square-foot expansion project was completed last year. The general contractor for that project was Willmeng Construction Inc., and the architect was Cawley Architects. Honeywell Aerospace has at least another nine years remaining on its Chandler lease. Honeywell has 9+ year lease remaining; invested $150M in renovations/40K SF expansion completed 2025

stories.summary: A Morgan Stanley Real Estate Investing affiliate purchased a nearly 200,000-square-foot industrial building in Chandler, Arizona for $59 million, where Honeywell Aerospace has been a tenant since 2020. Honeywell has invested roughly $150 million in renovations and expansions over the years, completing a 40,000-square-foot expansion last year. The aerospace tenant has at least nine years remaining on its lease. Morgan Stanley was attracted to the infill location, power infrastructure, and proximity to a strong manufacturing base.
stories.impact: Honeywell's sustained and capital-intensive manufacturing footprint in Chandler signals stability in metro Phoenix's advanced manufacturing cluster, supporting sustained job growth and population in-migration in Chandler submarket. This underpins multifamily demand fundamentals; developers should monitor Chandler rental absorption and capture aerospace/defense supply-chain worker influx.

stories.title: SimonCRE Acquires WA Retail Plaza for $12M, Plans Redevelopment
stories.excerpt: Scottsdale, Arizona-based investor SimonCRE has acquired Island Plaza, a 92,112-square-foot shopping center located in Oak Harbor on Whidbey Island, with plans for redevelopment. SimonCRE has already signed a 23,666-square-foot lease with a national soft goods retailer for the center’s largest available space. Island Plaza currently has approximately 5,600 square feet of vacant space, along with a half-acre development pad. The seller is the Carl Freund Trust, which has owned the property since 1980. The 4.35-acre site has an assessed value of $4.8 million, reported the Puget Sound Business Journal. Island Plaza comprises two multi-tenant buildings and a .50-acre pad site. Current tenants include Haggen, Jersey Mike’s Subs and Maurices, among others. The acquisition expands SimonCRE’s presence in the Pacific Northwest. The company is also redeveloping a property in Spanaway into a grocery-anchored retail center. SimonCRE purchased the 89,000-square-foot Spanaway Plaza from Goodwill Industries of Tacoma for $10 million in 2024. bullets: SimonCRE acquires Island Plaza (Oak Harbor, Whidbey Island WA) for $12M; 92K SF shopping center

stories.summary: Scottsdale-based SimonCRE acquired Island Plaza in Oak Harbor, Whidbey Island (Washington) for $12 million, a 92,112-square-foot shopping center. SimonCRE has already secured a 23,666-square-foot lease from a national soft goods retailer. The 4.35-acre site has 5,600 square feet of vacant space and a half-acre development pad. The acquisition builds on SimonCRE's ongoing redevelopment of Spanaway Plaza (purchased 2024 for $10 million).
stories.impact: Limited direct multifamily relevance. However, retail redevelopment in secondary markets (Whidbey Island, Spanaway) may signal developer confidence in tier-2 suburban PNW markets; if grocery-anchored centers (as in Spanaway) are adding, this can support pedestrian density and mixed-use upside, but watch for whether retail draw actually supports resident capture in any future residential components.

stories.title: Apartment Property in Seattle’s First Hill Neighborhood Trades
stories.excerpt: Monticello, a 107-unit apartment community located at 415 Boren Ave in Seattle’s First Hill neighborhood, has been acquired by Nordic Partners Investments. Built in 1957, Monticello spans 42,342 net rentable square feet across 107 units in the heart of Seattle’s urban core. The off-market acquisition drew multiple competing offers, delivering Nordic Partners Investments a value-add multifamily asset with meaningful economic upside in one of the city’s most established neighborhoods. Located just east of downtown Seattle, First Hill is one of the city’s most walkable and densely populated neighborhoods, anchored by a major medical and institutional employment base alongside easy access to downtown and Capitol Hill. Dylan Simon, Jerrid Anderson, and JD Fuller of Kidder Mathews’ Simon | Anderson Multifamily Team represented the seller and sourced the buyer in the transaction. “Monticello is proof that capital is actively hunting for Seattle multifamily,” said JD Fuller, Associate Vice President at Kidder Mathews. If you’re reading about the multifamily industry, you should be in the room with its leaders. Connect Apartments brings together the executives featured in Connect CRE’s coverage for an afternoon of high-level insights and unmatched networking on September 22 at The Biltmore in LA. The post Apartment Property in Seattle’s First Hill Neighborhood Trades appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Nordic Partners Investments acquires Monticello, 107-unit apartment building at 415 Boren Ave, Seattle First Hill

stories.summary: Nordic Partners Investments acquired Monticello, a 107-unit apartment community built in 1957 at 415 Boren Avenue in Seattle's First Hill neighborhood. The off-market transaction drew multiple competing bids, signaling strong investor demand for value-add multifamily in established urban neighborhoods. First Hill is one of Seattle's most walkable and densely populated neighborhoods, anchored by major medical and institutional employment alongside downtown and Capitol Hill access.
stories.impact: Clear signal of capital redeployment into Seattle multifamily, particularly older stock in walkable urban neighborhoods with institutional employment anchors. First Hill's medical employment base (UW Medicine, Swedish, Harborview proximity) provides stable renter demand; active bidding war indicates cap rates may be tightening for core-plus assets in Seattle. Developers should monitor First Hill absorption and rental growth—strong fundamentals could justify new supply or adaptive reuse in adjacent submarkets.

stories.title: NCREIF Reports Improving Q2 Returns for Key Quarterly Indices
stories.excerpt: The National Council of Real Estate Investment Fiduciaries (NCREIF) reported improving returns for both of its key quarterly indices for the second quarter of 2026. The NCREIF Property Index posted a slightly higher unleveraged quarterly return along with the highest total return for the trailing four quarters since Q4 2022, while the NCREIF Fund Index – Open-end Diversified Core Equity (NFI-ODCE) posted a total return of 1.49% for Q2, up from 1.25% in Q1 and 1.03% a year ago. For the NPI, the total return of 1.29% consisted of an income return of 1.17% and a capital appreciation return of 0.12%. The unleveraged returns are value-weighted for the properties and are calculated before the impact of investment management advisory fees. The NFI-ODCE total return consisted of an income return of 1.02%, up slightly quarter-over-quarter and year-over-year, and an appreciation return of 0.47%, up from 0.24% in Q1 2026 and 0.01% in Q2 2025. The average quarterly total, income and appreciation returns are 1.95%, 1.62% and 0.33%, respectively, since inception in Q1 1978. The NPI includes 13,160 properties, totaling $943 billion in market value. The NFI-ODCE includes 25 funds totaling $280.4 billion of gross real estate assets and $223.7 billion of net assets. The post NCREIF Reports Improving Q2 Returns for Key Quarterly Indices appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: NCREIF NPI Q2 2026 total return 1.29% (income 1.17%, appreciation 0.12%); highest trailing 4Q return since Q4 2022
NFI-ODCE Q2 return 1.49% (income 1.02%, appreciation 0.47%); appreciation up from 0.24% Q1 2026
NPI covers 13.2K properties, $943B market value; improving returns across income and capital appreciation
stories.summary: The NCREIF Property Index posted a total return of 1.29% for Q2 2026 (1.17% income, 0.12% appreciation), marking the highest trailing four-quarter return since Q4 2022. The NCREIF Fund Index–Open-end Diversified Core Equity reported 1.49% total return, with appreciation jumping to 0.47% from 0.24% in Q1 2026. Both indices show improving performance driven by modest but accelerating capital appreciation alongside stable income returns.
stories.impact: Improving capital appreciation signals stabilizing valuations and cap-rate compression, favorable for refinancing and acquisition multiples. Higher trailing returns may accelerate institutional capital deployment into CRE, supporting financing availability for multifamily development. Monitor continued appreciation trend; sustained momentum could validate higher basis assumptions for new development underwriting and justify increased starts in supply-constrained markets.

stories.title: PCCP, Integrity Community Builders Form Build-to-Rent JV
stories.excerpt: Integrity Community Builders (ICB) and PCCP have formed a programmatic joint venture to develop build-to-rent (BTR) communities across the U.S., Commercial Observer can first report. The new JV will marry Houston-based ICB’s experience in land acquisition, development and construction with PCCP’s institutional investment expertise. As co-investors, the partners will deploy up to $200 million per year into BTR communities — comprising detached homes, townhomes and cottage-style rentals — in the markets ICB and its affiliates currently operate in. “We believe this venture allows us to scale our build-to-rent platform with the right asset-managing partner,” Chad Durham, vice president of BTR at ICB, said in a statement. “Together with PCCP, our goal is creating thoughtfully designed rental communities in up to 19 markets.” Jennifer Diaz, partner and head of multifamily for PCCP, said the partnership reflects a strategic focus for PCCP: expansion into BTR. “We are proud to partner with ICB as we seek to develop high-quality build-to-rent communities in attractive growth markets,” she said in a statement. Integrity Community Builders was founded in 2020, and has since built 22 communities with another five under construction. The firm has worked with PCCP in the past as a general contractor, having built several communities for PCCP. “We feel like we’ve developed a pretty good brand and reputation in the space as a developer and builder, but serving clients like PCCP and other sponsors is really what we’d been doing,” Durham said. “We knew that we wouldn’t be able to control our growth and get to the number of units a year that we’d like to be building — which is 1,500, plus or minus — by just depending on other sponsors bringing us projects to build, or going into the market and trying to find sponsors on projects that we’ve sourced. bullets: PCCP and Integrity Community Builders (Houston) form BTR JV; deploy up to $200M/year build-to-rent
Target: detached homes, townhomes, cottages across up to 19 markets where ICB currently operates
PCCP expands multifamily platform into BTR as strategic priority; marriage of ICB land/construction expertise + PCCP capital
stories.summary: Integrity Community Builders and PCCP have formed a joint venture to develop build-to-rent communities nationwide, committing up to $200 million per year. The partnership combines ICB's land acquisition, development, and construction experience with PCCP's institutional investment expertise. The JV will build detached homes, townhomes, and cottage-style rentals across up to 19 markets in which ICB and affiliates currently operate.
stories.impact: Significant capital reallocation signal: $200M/year BTR deployment indicates institutional conviction that single-family rental offers higher risk-adjusted returns than traditional apartment development in ICB's footprint. BTR scale-up may increase competition for suburban infill land and shift price expectations; multifamily developers should monitor which of ICB's 19 markets (likely Sun Belt + growth metros) are receiving BTR capital and watch for pricing pressure on comparable land sites. BTR supply growth may also cannibalize entry-level renter demand.

stories.title: CMBS Loan Backed by Pittsburgh’s Gateway Center Liquidates at $65M Loss
stories.excerpt: An iconic office complex in the City of Bridges has hit a dead end. The $92 million commercial mortgage-backed securities (CMBS) loan secured by Gateway Center, an iconic office complex in Downtown Pittsburgh, has liquidated via a note sale, resulting in a $64.8 million loss to the CMBS trust, according to an alert from Morningstar Credit. CO previously reported that the $94 million loan — which makes up 64 percent of the JPMCC 2013-C10 conduit deal — entered special servicing in September 2024 after it was expected to default ahead of its January 2025 maturity. Gateway Center’s four office buildings reported occupancy as low as 55 percent in March 2024. Morningstar Credit reported the gross proceeds were a mere $37.4 million, well below the previously appraised value of $69.5 million. Within the trust, two tranches were written off completely, while the Class E junior tranche lost half its value, per Morningstar. The office complex was purchased by Hertz Investment Group in 2004 for $55 million. A product of the postwar era boom of Brutalist architecture, Gateway Center has formed an indelible piece of the Pittsburgh skyline since the early 1950s, when construction of the buildings was complete. Spanning 1.5 million square feet of office space across One Gateway Center, Two Gateway Center, Three Gateway Center and Four Gateway Center, the stainless steel and glass development opened in stages between 1952 and 1960. The development was part of the “Pittsburgh Renaissance” that occurred between 1946 and 1974. At the time, the 23-acre Gateway Center commercial district was known as “the nation’s first comprehensive downtown redevelopment accomplished without federal aid,” according to the Pittsburgh History & Landmarks Foundation. bullets: Gateway Center Pittsburgh CMBS loan liquidates at $64.8M loss; $92M loan, $37.4M gross proceeds
Occupancy as low as 55% March 2024; appraised at $69.5M, sold for $37.4M; office distress signal
Two CMBS tranches written off; Class E junior tranche lost 50% value; JPMCC 2013-C10 impaired
stories.summary: The $92 million CMBS loan secured by Gateway Center, an iconic four-building office complex in Downtown Pittsburgh, has liquidated via note sale, resulting in a $64.8 million loss to the trust. Gross proceeds totaled $37.4 million, far below the $69.5 million appraised value. The property reported occupancy as low as 55% in March 2024. Two tranches were written off entirely, and the Class E junior tranche lost half its value.
stories.impact: Severe office distress in secondary markets (Pittsburgh) highlights risk of legacy office buildings with weak tenant demand and aging stock. Minimal direct multifamily impact, but underscores capital flight from office; reallocated CMBS capital may favor multifamily and industrial. Pittsburgh office weakness does NOT signal apartment demand; monitor whether office-to-residential conversion gains traction as an alternative use (redemption mechanism for distressed assets).

stories.title: Muji, Daniel Eddy’s Winner Sign Retail Leases at Brooklyn’s Alloy Block
stories.excerpt: Two new retail tenants have taken almost 13,000 square feet at a new development in Downtown Brooklyn. Japanese home goods and apparel brand Muji was the largest of the two, signing a 10-year, 10,000-square-foot lease at Alloy Development’s 100 Flatbush Avenue, part of the larger five-building, mixed-use Alloy Block complex, according to the landlord. Retail asking rents in the development are $225 per square foot for street-level space and $75 per square foot for space in the lower level, according to Alloy Development. “Every new Muji store is an investment in the communities we serve,” Richard Rappaport, president of Muji USA, said in a statement. “Downtown Brooklyn’s continued growth, diversity and energy make it an ideal place for us to expand our presence and reach even more customers.” Chris DeCrosta, Hank O’Donnell and Madeleine Naro of Goodspace NYC negotiated on behalf of the landlord in both deals, while Cushman & Wakefield’s Jason Greenstone, Mike O’Neill, Taylor Reynolds and Lilly Craver represented Muji. Muji will open in 2027. C&W declined to comment on the transaction, while the GoodSpace NYC team did not immediately respond to a request for comment. In addition, a cafe and bakery known as Winner by Michelin-star chef Daniel Eddy signed a 10-year, 2,726-square-foot lease for the concept’s second location at Alloy Block. The cafe will serve a mix of Parisian and Nicaraguan baked goods. Winner did not use any brokers in the negotiations, according to Alloy, and it will open in the fall. Meanwhile, sports card and collectible retailer CardVault by Tom Brady in March also opened a 973-square-foot store at 80 Flatbush Avenue, another component of Alloy Block. The Block complex also includes the all-electric tower 505 State Street and One Third Avenue. Mark Hallum can be reached at mhallum@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Muji signs 10K SF, 10-year lease at 100 Flatbush Ave, Alloy Block Brooklyn; 2 tenants ~13K SF total
Street-level rents $225/SF, lower-level $75/SF; Alloy Development five-building mixed-use complex
Downtown Brooklyn continued growth/diversity cited by Muji; new retail leasing activity in dense urban development
stories.summary: Japanese home-goods and apparel brand Muji signed a 10,000-square-foot, 10-year lease at Alloy Development's 100 Flatbush Avenue in Downtown Brooklyn as part of the larger Alloy Block mixed-use complex. A second tenant, Daniel Eddy's Winner, also signed, together leasing nearly 13,000 square feet. Retail asking rents are $225 per square foot for street-level and $75 per square foot for lower-level space.
stories.impact: Downtown Brooklyn retail leasing momentum signals continued mixed-use urban density and pedestrian demand, supporting multifamily fundamentals in the submarket. Muji's anchor presence and premium rents ($225/SF street-level) indicate landlord confidence and strong foot traffic—positive signal for adjacent residential projects. However, this is primarily a retail lead; monitor whether Alloy Block's mixed-use program includes multifamily and whether retail-anchored density translates into renter capture.

stories.title: Visual Effects Studio Phosphene Takes 7K SF at 90 Broad Street
stories.excerpt: Emmy nominated visual effects studio Phosphene has inked a 7,383-square-foot lease at Princeton International’s 90 Broad Street in Manhattan’s Financial District, according to tenant broker Avison Young. Phosphene will move from its current office at 5 Hanover Square, also in the Financial District, as the building is being converted from an office property into a residential tower. The asking rent and the length of the lease were not disclosed. The average asking rent for office space in Lower Manhattan was $63.76 during the second quarter of 2026, according to data from Colliers. Oliver Petrovic and Story Langston from Avison Young represented Phosphene in the lease, while Jon Fein from Cushman & Wakefield represented the landlord. “The conversion pipeline is steadily reducing the supply of office space, making it increasingly important for tenants to plan ahead and act decisively,” Petrovic said in a statement. “For this client, the relocation became an opportunity to create a purpose-built environment that better aligns with the needs of a growing post-production company.” C&W did not immediately respond to Commercial Observer’s request for comment. “The challenge of moving a visual effects studio is always an underestimated real estate task,” Vivian Connolly, CEO of Phosphene, said in a statement. “Oliver and his team understood the task at hand and navigated the New York City real estate climate intelligently and efficiently. We are looking forward to our new and improved fully customized space.” Built in 1932, 90 Broad Street spans a full block between Stone and Bridge streets. Other tenants in the building include law firm Sher Termonte and STEM nonprofit BEAM. Amanda Schiavo can be reached at aschiavo@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Phosphene visual effects studio leases 7.4K SF at 90 Broad Street, Financial District Manhattan
Relocating from 5 Hanover Square (being converted office-to-residential); Lower Manhattan office rents $63.76/SF Q2 2026
Conversion pipeline reducing office supply; tenants forced to relocate and plan ahead proactively
stories.summary: Emmy-nominated visual effects studio Phosphene has leased 7,383 square feet at Princeton International's 90 Broad Street in Manhattan's Financial District. Phosphene is relocating from 5 Hanover Square, which is being converted from office to residential use. Lower Manhattan office average rents are $63.76 per square foot as of Q2 2026.
stories.impact: Conversion pipeline in Lower Manhattan is actively displacing office tenants and shrinking usable office stock, creating tailwinds for residential conversion projects. Tenants being forced to relocate and "plan ahead decisively" signals tightening office availability and rising dislocation costs, which favor near-term residential conversion economics. Developers with conversion-ready Lower Manhattan office assets should prioritize conversion underwriting; demand for residential in FiDi remains supported by ferry/subway access and young professional demographic.
